title: Paired before/after boxplots in R with canvasXpress
text: When the same subjects are measured twice — before/after a treatment, baseline vs follow-up — a paired boxplot with a line connecting each subject across the two timepoints tells the story a plain boxplot can’t. This post builds one in R by wrapping a ggpubr ggpaired plot with canvasXpress, so it becomes interactive and reproducible without re-specifying anything.

title: Paired before/after boxplots in R with canvasXpress
text:
Install

install.packages(c("canvasXpress", "ggpubr"))

title: Paired before/after boxplots in R with canvasXpress
text:
A paired dataset
Long format, two rows per subject — one per timepoint. Swap in your own repeated-measures table.

library(ggplot2)
library(ggpubr)

set.seed(7)
n  <- 25
df <- data.frame(
  id    = rep(paste0("P", seq_len(n)), 2),
  time  = rep(c("Baseline", "Week 12"), each = n),
  value = c(rnorm(n, 8, 1.2),                       # baseline
            rnorm(n, 8, 1.2) + rnorm(n, -1.2, 0.8)) # follow-up (a drop)
)

title: Paired before/after boxplots in R with canvasXpress
section: Build it with ggpaired, then wrap it
text:
Build it with ggpaired, then wrap it
ggpaired draws the two boxes and the per-subject connecting lines; stat_compare_means adds a paired test. Then hand the whole thing to canvasXpress():

library(canvasXpress)

g <- ggpaired(
  df, x = "time", y = "value", id = "id",
  color = "time", line.color = "gray", line.size = 0.3
) +
  stat_compare_means(paired = TRUE, method = "t.test")

canvasXpress(g)





Each grey line is one subject moving from Baseline to Week 12, the boxes summarize each timepoint, and the paired t-test labels the comparison. It’s interactive — hover a line to follow a subject — and the figure is one portable spec you can reproduce from R, Python or JavaScript.

title: Paired before/after boxplots in R with canvasXpress
section: Why paired, not two independent boxes
text:
Why paired, not two independent boxes
A side-by-side boxplot hides who changed. The connecting lines make within-subject change visible: a treatment can lower the group median while a handful of subjects still rise — exactly the pattern you want to catch before drawing conclusions.

title: Clustered heatmaps in R with canvasXpress
text: The clustered heatmap is the default way to look at an expression matrix: rows and columns reordered by similarity, dendrograms on the margins, and sample metadata alongside. In this post we build one in R with canvasXpress — clustering happens inside the render, so you pass a plain matrix and get an interactive, reproducible figure.

title: Clustered heatmaps in R with canvasXpress
section: An expression matrix with sample metadata
text:
An expression matrix with sample metadata
Swap this simulated block for your own matrix (genes in rows, samples in columns) and a table of per-sample annotations — the output of any normalization/DE pipeline works.

library(canvasXpress)

set.seed(1)
ng    <- 40                       # genes (rows)
ns    <- 30                       # samples (columns)
genes <- paste0("Gene", seq_len(ng))
samps <- paste0("S", seq_len(ns))
cond  <- rep(c("Tumor", "Normal"), each = ns / 2)

# Two gene blocks, up in one condition each
m <- matrix(rnorm(ng * ns), ng, ns, dimnames = list(genes, samps))
m[ 1:20, cond == "Tumor"]  <- m[ 1:20, cond == "Tumor"]  + 2
m[21:40, cond == "Normal"] <- m[21:40, cond == "Normal"] + 2

canvasXpress takes the matrix as data and a sample annotation table (rows = samples) that becomes an annotation track over the columns.

smpAnnot <- data.frame(Condition = cond, row.names = samps, check.names = FALSE)

title: Clustered heatmaps in R with canvasXpress
text:
The plot
samplesClustered and variablesClustered turn on hierarchical clustering (with dendrograms) on columns and rows; colorSpectrum sets the diverging palette.

canvasXpress(
  data     = as.data.frame(m),
  smpAnnot = smpAnnot,
  graphType = "Heatmap",
  samplesClustered  = TRUE,
  variablesClustered = TRUE,
  colorSpectrum = list("navy", "white", "firebrick3"),
  showSmpDendrogram = TRUE,
  showVarDendrogram = TRUE,
  title = "Clustered expression heatmap",
  width  = 650,
  height = 550
)





The rows and columns are reordered by similarity, the dendrograms show the clustering, and the samples separate cleanly by condition. Hover a cell for its gene, sample and value; the whole figure is one portable spec you can store, validate and re-render.

title: Clustered heatmaps in R with canvasXpress
text:
Scaling up
The same call handles much larger matrices — hundreds of genes by dozens to hundreds of samples — clustering and rendering the full matrix interactively in the browser, not a static image. Point size and labels adapt automatically.

title: Kaplan–Meier survival curves in R with canvasXpress
text: Kaplan–Meier curves summarize time-to-event data: the step-down survival probability over time, usually split by a group like treatment arm. In this post we build one in R with canvasXpress. canvasXpress computes the survival steps for you — you hand it a time column and a censoring column, and it does the rest — and the result is an interactive figure that serializes to one portable, reproducible spec.

title: Kaplan–Meier survival curves in R with canvasXpress
text:
A survival table
Swap this simulated block for your own data: you need, per subject, a follow-up time, a censoring indicator (1 = censored, 0 = event), and the grouping variable.

library(canvasXpress)

set.seed(1)
n    <- 200
arm  <- sample(c("Treatment", "Control"), n, replace = TRUE)
base <- ifelse(arm == "Treatment", 60, 40)      # treatment survives longer
time <- round(rexp(n, rate = 1 / base), 1)
cens <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.3)                        # 1 = censored, 0 = event
subj <- paste0("Subj", seq_len(n))

canvasXpress reads two columns for a Kaplan–Meier plot — the time and its matching censor flag — plus a per-subject annotation carrying the group.

y <- data.frame(
  "Time"        = time,
  "Time-Censor" = cens,
  row.names     = subj,
  check.names   = FALSE
)

varAnnot <- data.frame(Arm = arm, row.names = subj, check.names = FALSE)

title: Kaplan–Meier survival curves in R with canvasXpress
text:
The plot
The key is graphType = "KaplanMeier" and passing both columns to xAxis (time first, then the censor column). colorBy stratifies the curves.

canvasXpress(
  data     = y,
  varAnnot = varAnnot,
  graphType = "KaplanMeier",
  xAxis    = list("Time", "Time-Censor"),
  colorBy  = "Arm",
  title    = "Overall survival by treatment arm",
  xAxisTitle = "Time (weeks)",
  yAxisTitle = "Probability of survival",
  invertCensored = TRUE,     # draw censoring ticks
  showKMConfidenceIntervals = FALSE,
  width  = 650,
  height = 500
)





Hover any step for the time and survival probability; the tick marks are censored subjects. Because canvasXpress derives the survival curve from the raw table, you never precompute the steps — and the same spec re-renders the identical curve from Python or JavaScript.

title: Kaplan–Meier survival curves in R with canvasXpress
text:
A common gotcha
The survival transform only fires with graphType = "KaplanMeier". If you use a bare "Scatter2D" you’ll get a raw scatter of the censor values instead — survival probability is computed by the engine, it is not a column in your data.

title: Kaplan–Meier survival curves in Python with canvasxpress
text: Kaplan–Meier curves summarize time-to-event data: the step-down survival probability over time, usually split by a group like treatment arm. Here we build one in Python with canvasxpress — it computes the survival steps for you from a time column and a censoring column — and the result is interactive and reproducible.

title: Kaplan–Meier survival curves in Python with canvasxpress
text:
Install
pip install canvasxpress

title: Kaplan–Meier survival curves in Python with canvasxpress
text:
A survival table
Swap this simulated block for your own data: per subject you need a follow-up time, a censoring indicator (1 = censored, 0 = event), and the grouping variable.

import numpy as np

rng  = np.random.default_rng(1)
n    = 200
arm  = rng.choice(["Treatment", "Control"], n)
base = np.where(arm == "Treatment", 60, 40)     # treatment survives longer
time = np.round(rng.exponential(base), 1)
cens = rng.binomial(1, 0.3, n)                  # 1 = censored, 0 = event
subj = [f"Subj{i+1}" for i in range(n)]

title: Kaplan–Meier survival curves in Python with canvasxpress
text:
Build the spec
The two columns — the time and its matching censor flag — go in as the variable samples, and the arm rides along as a variable annotation. The key is graphType="KaplanMeier" and passing both columns to xAxis.

from canvasxpress.canvas import CanvasXpress
from canvasxpress.render.jupyter import CXNoteBook
from IPython.display import display

data = {
    "y": {"vars": ["Time", "Time-Censor"], "smps": subj,
          "data": [time.tolist(), cens.tolist()]},
    "z": {"Arm": arm.tolist()},
}

config = {
    "graphType": "KaplanMeier",
    "xAxis": ["Time", "Time-Censor"],
    "colorBy": "Arm",
    "title": "Overall survival by treatment arm",
    "xAxisTitle": "Time (weeks)", "yAxisTitle": "Probability of survival",
    "invertCensored": True,               # draw censoring ticks
    "showKMConfidenceIntervals": False,
}

cx = CanvasXpress(render_to="km", data=data, config=config, width=650, height=500)
for part in CXNoteBook(cx).render():
    display(part)






  






Hover any step for the time and survival probability; the tick marks are censored subjects. canvasxpress derives the survival curve from the raw table, so you never precompute the steps — and the same spec re-renders the identical curve from R or JavaScript.

title: Kaplan–Meier survival curves in Python with canvasxpress
text:
A common gotcha
The survival transform only fires with graphType="KaplanMeier". A bare "Scatter2D" gives a raw scatter of the censor values instead — survival probability is computed by the engine, not a column in your data.

Here we build one in Python with canvasxpress — clustering happens inside the render, so you pass a plain matrix and get an interactive, reproducible figure.

title: Clustered heatmaps in Python with canvasxpress
text:
Install
pip install canvasxpress

title: Clustered heatmaps in Python with canvasxpress
section: An expression matrix with sample metadata
text:
An expression matrix with sample metadata
Swap this simulated block for your own matrix (genes in rows, samples in columns) and a table of per-sample annotations.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng   = np.random.default_rng(1)
ng, ns = 40, 30
genes = [f"Gene{i+1}" for i in range(ng)]
samps = [f"S{i+1}"    for i in range(ns)]
cond  = ["Tumor"] * (ns // 2) + ["Normal"] * (ns // 2)

m = rng.normal(0, 1, (ng, ns))
tumor = [i for i, c in enumerate(cond) if c == "Tumor"]
normal = [i for i, c in enumerate(cond) if c == "Normal"]
m[np.ix_(range(0, 20),  tumor)]  += 2      # first block up in Tumor
m[np.ix_(range(20, 40), normal)] += 2      # second block up in Normal

expr = pd.DataFrame(m.round(3), index=genes, columns=samps)

title: Clustered heatmaps in Python with canvasxpress
text:
Build the spec
The matrix goes in as data, and the sample annotation becomes an annotation track over the columns. samplesClustered / variablesClustered turn on hierarchical clustering with dendrograms.

from canvasxpress.canvas import CanvasXpress
from canvasxpress.render.jupyter import CXNoteBook
from IPython.display import display

data = {
    "y": {"vars": genes, "smps": samps, "data": expr.values.tolist()},
    "x": {"Condition": cond},
}

config = {
    "graphType": "Heatmap",
    "samplesClustered": True, "variablesClustered": True,
    "colorSpectrum": ["navy", "white", "firebrick3"],
    "showSmpDendrogram": True, "showVarDendrogram": True,
    "title": "Clustered expression heatmap",
}

cx = CanvasXpress(render_to="heatmap", data=data, config=config, width=650, height=550)
for part in CXNoteBook(cx).render():
    display(part)






  






Rows and columns are reordered by similarity, the dendrograms show the clustering, and the samples separate cleanly by condition. Hover a cell for its gene, sample and value; the whole figure is one portable spec you can store, validate and re-render from R or JavaScript.

title: Interactive volcano plots in Python with canvasxpress
text: A volcano plot is the workhorse of differential-expression analysis: log fold change on x, statistical significance on y, and the interesting genes pushed to the top corners. Here we build one in Python with canvasxpress — interactive (zoom, hover, filter) and reproducible: the whole figure is one portable specification you can store and re-render from Python, R or JavaScript.

title: Interactive volcano plots in Python with canvasxpress
text:
Install
pip install canvasxpress

title: Interactive volcano plots in Python with canvasxpress
text:
A differential-expression table
Swap this simulated block for your own results — the output of any DE pipeline works, as long as you have a log fold change and a significance value per gene.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 1000
genes   = [f"Gene{i+1}" for i in range(n)]
logfc   = rng.normal(0, 0.8, n)
neglogp = -np.log10(rng.uniform(size=n) ** 1.5)   # stand-in for -log10(p-value)

df = pd.DataFrame({"logFC": logfc.round(3), "-log-pVal": neglogp.round(3)}, index=genes)

def classify(fc, p):
    if fc > 1 and p > 2:   return "Increased"
    if fc < -1 and p > 2:  return "Decreased"
    return "NoChange"

group = [classify(fc, p) for fc, p in zip(df["logFC"], df["-log-pVal"])]
fold  = (2 ** df["logFC"].abs()).round(2)

title: Interactive volcano plots in Python with canvasxpress
text:
Build the spec
canvasxpress takes a data object (a value matrix plus annotations) and a config. We put the two measurements as the variable’s samples and carry the regulation call and fold change as variable annotations (z).

from canvasxpress.canvas import CanvasXpress
from canvasxpress.render.jupyter import CXNoteBook
from IPython.display import display

data = {
    "y": {"vars": ["logFC", "-log-pVal"], "smps": genes,
          "data": [df["logFC"].tolist(), df["-log-pVal"].tolist()]},
    "z": {"Group": group, "FC": fold.tolist()},
}

config = {
    "graphType": "Scatter2D",
    "title": "Publication-ready volcano plot",
    "xAxis": ["logFC"], "yAxis": ["-log-pVal"],
    "xAxisTitle": "log2 fold change", "yAxisTitle": "-log10 p-value",
    "colorBy": "Group",
    "colorKey": {"Group": {"Increased": "rgba(197,27,38,0.75)",
                            "Decreased": "rgba(33,102,172,0.75)",
                            "NoChange":  "rgba(150,150,150,0.35)"}},
    "sizeBy": "FC", "sizes": [3, 6, 9, 12, 15],
    "showDecorations": True,
    "decorations": {"line": [
        {"color": "rgba(120,120,120,0.8)", "width": 1, "x": 1},
        {"color": "rgba(120,120,120,0.8)", "width": 1, "x": -1},
        {"color": "rgba(120,120,120,0.8)", "width": 1, "y": 1.301},
    ]},
}

cx = CanvasXpress(render_to="volcano", data=data, config=config, width=650, height=500)
for part in CXNoteBook(cx).render():
    display(part)






  






The chart is interactive — hover a point for its gene and values, drag to zoom, filter by regulation group in the toolbar. The dashed guides mark the ±1 log2FC and p = 0.05 cutoffs.

title: Interactive volcano plots in Python with canvasxpress
text:
Why “reproducible”
Everything above serializes to one JSON specification — the data and the config. That spec is portable: the identical figure renders from the R (canvasXpress) and JavaScript packages, and it can be validated against a published schema and re-rendered later, so a figure in a paper can be regenerated and audited rather than just viewed.

title: Use your ggplot2 (and ggpubr) plots directly with canvasXpress
text: If you already build plots with ggplot2 or ggpubr, you don’t need to learn a new plotting API to make them interactive. canvasXpress accepts a ggplot object directly: pass it to canvasXpress() and it renders an interactive, reproducible version of the same figure — you keep your existing code.

title: Use your ggplot2 (and ggpubr) plots directly with canvasXpress
text:
Install

install.packages(c("canvasXpress", "ggpubr"))

title: Use your ggplot2 (and ggpubr) plots directly with canvasXpress
section: Wrap a plot you already have
text:
Wrap a plot you already have
Here’s an ordinary ggpubr boxplot with pairwise comparisons (geom_pwc) — the significance brackets that show a test between each pair of groups. Build it exactly as you normally would:

library(ggplot2)
library(ggpubr)

g <- ggboxplot(iris, x = "Species", y = "Sepal.Width", fill = "Species") +
  geom_pwc(method = "t_test", label = "p.format")

Now make it interactive — one call, the same object:

library(canvasXpress)

canvasXpress(g)





That’s the whole idea: no re-specification. canvasXpress reads the ggplot object — its data, aesthetics, layers, scales and the geom_pwc brackets — and renders it. Hover the points, drag to zoom, or open the toolbar to filter and re-style, and the result serializes to one portable spec you can store and reproduce from R, Python or JavaScript.

title: Use your ggplot2 (and ggpubr) plots directly with canvasXpress
text:
What transfers

Geoms and layers — points, boxes, lines, and stats like geom_pwc / stat_compare_means.
Aesthetic mappings — x, y, fill, color, grouping.
Scales, labels and facets from the ggplot object.

title: Use your ggplot2 (and ggpubr) plots directly with canvasXpress
section: When to reach for the native API instead
text:
When to reach for the native API instead
Wrapping a ggplot is ideal for reusing plots you already have. When you’re building a figure fresh — or want fine control over CanvasXpress-specific features (clustering, dendrograms, interactive annotations) — call canvasXpress() on your data directly with a graphType. See the other posts for that style.

title: Interactive volcano plots in R with canvasXpress
text: A volcano plot is the workhorse of differential-expression analysis: log fold change on x, statistical significance on y, and the interesting genes pushed out to the top corners. In this post we build one in R with canvasXpress — interactive (zoom, hover, filter), and, importantly, reproducible: the whole figure is a single portable specification you can store, validate and re-render from R, Python or JavaScript.

title: Interactive volcano plots in R with canvasXpress
text:
Install

install.packages("canvasXpress")

title: Interactive volcano plots in R with canvasXpress
text:
A differential-expression table
For a self-contained example we simulate 1,000 genes. Swap this block for your own results table (e.g. the output of limma::topTable() or DESeq2::results()) — you need a log fold change and a significance value per gene.

library(canvasXpress)

set.seed(1)
n       <- 1000
genes   <- paste0("Gene", seq_len(n))
logFC   <- rnorm(n, 0, 0.8)
negLogP <- -log10(runif(n)^1.5)   # stand-in for -log10(p-value)

# Classify each gene by effect size + significance
group <- ifelse(logFC >  1 & negLogP > 2, "Increased",
         ifelse(logFC < -1 & negLogP > 2, "Decreased", "NoChange"))

canvasXpress expects a numeric matrix/data frame of values (genes in rows) plus an optional variable annotation table carrying per-gene attributes — here the regulation call and the fold change we’ll use for point size.

y <- data.frame(
  "logFC"     = logFC,
  "-log-pVal" = negLogP,
  row.names   = genes,
  check.names = FALSE
)

varAnnot <- data.frame(
  Group = group,
  FC    = round(2^abs(logFC), 2),
  row.names   = genes,
  check.names = FALSE
)

title: Interactive volcano plots in R with canvasXpress
text:
The plot

canvasXpress(
  data     = y,
  varAnnot = varAnnot,
  graphType = "Scatter2D",
  xAxis    = list("logFC"),
  yAxis    = list("-log-pVal"),
  colorBy  = "Group",
  colorKey = list(Group = list(
    Increased = "rgba(197,27,38,0.75)",
    Decreased = "rgba(33,102,172,0.75)",
    NoChange  = "rgba(150,150,150,0.35)"
  )),
  sizeBy   = "FC",
  sizes    = c(3, 6, 9, 12, 15),
  title    = "Publication-ready volcano plot",
  xAxisTitle = "log2 fold change",
  yAxisTitle = "-log10 p-value",
  showDecorations = TRUE,
  decorations = list(line = list(
    list(color = "rgba(120,120,120,0.8)", width = 1, x =  1),
    list(color = "rgba(120,120,120,0.8)", width = 1, x = -1),
    list(color = "rgba(120,120,120,0.8)", width = 1, y = 1.301)
  )),
  width  = 650,
  height = 500
)





The chart is interactive: hover a point for its gene and values, drag to zoom, or use the toolbar to filter by regulation group. The dashed guides mark the ±1 log2FC and the p = 0.05 cutoffs.

title: Interactive volcano plots in R with canvasXpress
text:
Why “reproducible”
Everything above serializes to one JSON specification — the data and the config. That spec is portable: the identical figure renders from the Python (canvasxpress) and JavaScript packages, and it can be validated against a published schema and re-rendered later, so a figure in a paper can be regenerated and audited rather than just looked at.

title: About
text:
This blog covers interactive, reproducible scientific visualization in R with canvasXpress — the R interface to the CanvasXpress engine.
The idea in one line: a figure is a portable JSON specification (data + config). The same spec renders identically from R, Python and JavaScript, and can be stored, validated, compared and reproduced — so a plot behaves like code.

Package (CRAN): install.packages("canvasXpress")
Source & issues: github.com/neuhausi/canvasXpress
Gallery and docs: canvasxpress.org

Posts here are hands-on R recipes: paste one, swap in your data.
